Iamblichus of Chalcis in Coele-Syria, On the Common Mathematical Science: third discourse. Translated from the Greek text of Nicola Festa (Leipzig, 1891). The numbers in the margin are Festa’s pages, the standard reference for this work.
Chapter 1

What the purpose of the present book is as a whole, and what the particular aims falling under it are, in how many ways and into what they are divided, and whence and from what kind of essence they derive the first causes of the inquiry appropriate to them.

The purpose of the present inquiry is to set forth the common theory of the mathematical sciences: what it is as a whole, and what single cause and most senior essence it has going before it; and we shall examine whether, after the single cause, there are in some way two principles of it; and after this dichotomy we shall try to reckon up, by means of a certain scientific division, whether there is any determinate number of the genera in them; and then indeed we shall examine the common forms of all the mathematical sciences by a certain common approach, not yet touching upon the theorems of each in particular. Under each of the points mentioned we shall set forth the essence in which each genus and species of mathematical objects is present; and we shall not omit to say what their contribution to the whole is and their ordering in relation to one another, what kinship they have and whence it comes to them, from what principles it is bound together, to what causes senior to itself it is led up, and how one might be able to attain them, in what respect the study is useful and to how many goods it leads the way, and that it is choiceworthy both for itself and on account of the sciences that arise from it, and that it turns discursive thought round towards all philosophy and towards the whole science of beings and intelligibles.
Such in number, then, are the matters set before us to go through in this book; let us begin from the first, taking it up from the beginning.

In common, then, concerning all the mathematical sciences, let these axioms be laid down by us: that they are incorporeal and subsist in themselves, intermediate between the indivisible essences and those divisible about bodies, between forms and reason-principles, having been allotted the rank between the partless and the divisible, being purer than the latter and more variegated than the former; employing composition and division, yet surveying what is composed and divided in an ungenerated and eternal manner; being inferior to the intelligible essences, but prior to those in nature; surpassing visible things in beauty, order and exactness, but falling short of the intelligibles; employing likewise an intermediate commensurability and agreement; and having the power to ferry and convey across to the indivisible forms, inasmuch as they are akin to them, both leading those who become habituated to them away from bodies and turning them round towards the divine essences as by a kind of ladder leading up to the height. One must, then, view the secondary gift of the essence of incorporeals as coming down into these not from one genus of beings only, but from all the genera whatsoever that exist in that which truly is and in intellect; for from all of these there descends into the intermediate natures of the mathematical sciences the mean between the causes and the things brought to completion by them, and it joins the things that come to be to the things that are and produces a communion of them with one another.

Since, then, the theory of the mathematical sciences is of such scope and extends in this way to all things, mathematical science is an intermediate knowledge, exceeding intellect in composition, being of a discursive kind, comprehending many things in the same, making use rather of certain traversals and unfoldings, and of forms and reason-principles that are intermediate and not in every way limited, but which mark off the limit about the unlimited and furnish clarity in matters not very well known.
Chapter 2

What the common theory is concerning the mathematical sciences as a whole and concerning mathematical science, and whence one must grasp it and from what things one must take its defining limit, and how great an extent it has, reaching to how many common genera.

The science being of this kind, then, one must grasp it by standing apart from bodies and generation, keeping pure of imaginations and sense-perceptions, habituating oneself to things incorporeal in themselves, and making continual use of the exercise of reasonings. And it is right to set the defining limit upon them from the science of beings and the pure intellection of the pure reason-principles, the immaterial forms and the limited truth of the intelligibles; for from these one would acquire in addition the perfection and purity of the knowledge that is in them. It extends to all the genera and species of beings that are intermediate, both those that are comprehended in determinate numbers and those that proceed in a determinate manner according to certain formal differences. And some advance forward and ascend to the height, others draw near to things inferior and lower, while those that are in the middle between these join the extremes.

Their genera and species must be distinguished according to all these, and further they must be divided into some as existing in themselves and others as relative to other things; and their distinction must be understood also according to the differences of quantity, and according to the divisions of the intermediate reason-principles and forms; and some of them must be posited as prior, others as posterior, according as their natures have their ordering relative to one another. One can also infer their otherness according to the cognitive faculties of the soul, all those that are intermediate and discursive, as Archytas too evidently does in the section of the cognitive line. Let such, to sketch it in outline, be the first comprehensive account of the common theory concerning the mathematical sciences; and from this point, taking the matter up again from the beginning, let us try to go through one by one the problems already stated.
Chapter 3

What the principles of the mathematical sciences as a whole are, and in what respect they differ from the other principles, all those that are principles of other essences, and how such principles furnish their cause in common to the mathematical sciences as a whole.

Let us, then, determine in common for all the mathematical sciences what the principles of mathematical essence are; for since every science comes about through its own principles, the best knowledge of mathematical essence too would be that which sets out from there. Now that the limited and the unlimited are principles of all the mathematical sciences and of all mathematical essence is clear to everyone, as the Pythagoreans hold; but each of these does not have a single account, nor the same one in every essence: rather, in the case of the intelligible forms and the immaterial reason-principles such principles are different, being intelligible in every way and immaterial and in themselves indivisible, whereas in the case of the mathematical sciences they will be causes of multitude and magnitude, of division and extension, and will partake of divisible nature and take on genera of their own, those appropriate to the mathematical sciences as a whole, and will have a share in composition and will be judged by a discursive thinking that is other than the faculty which judges the simple, indivisible and intellective essences.

Some will perhaps assign motion to these principles of the mathematical sciences, namely all those who posit these principles in the soul and in the lives and powers of the soul; but it is better to place the soul in another genus of essence, and to suppose the mathematical principles and mathematical essence to be unmoved; for their forms stand always fixed, and we contemplate them in the same way and in the same respects. These principles of the unlimited and of limit, then, are of an intermediate kind, the form of limit always prevailing over that of the unlimited and bounding it within itself; hence too there is always procession towards the unlimited, but determination by that which limits. From the reason-principles that exist in intellect, then, these principles differ in that they give forth from themselves the cause of division, multitude, magnitude and composition; while from those of nature and those of soul they are separated both by being unmoved and because they belong to the intermediate incorporeals ranked in between and exist by themselves separated from matter, whereas those others also lay hold of matter. That they differ, then, from the other causes, one may be persuaded from these considerations.

Their community, which extends to all, must be understood from the mean conceived thus without qualification, and from the nature that is inferior to the indivisible and intelligible forms but senior to those divisible about bodies. And if one should take reason-principles, it is according to this that their community in the reason-principles must be contemplated. And indeterminacy too must likewise be posited as extending in common to all. And if certain receptacles of the mathematical forms are conceived, it is right to leave these as common to the whole multiform constitution observed in the mathematical sciences; for in this way one might comprehend their community, which is hard to grasp in thought so as to embrace it in a single reasoning, because it is present in many and differing things, but which might with difficulty be conceived in this way. Let so much, then, be determined by us concerning the common principles as well.
Chapter 4

What the proper principles of each of the mathematical sciences are, and what distinctive property they have in themselves, what difference from one another, and what difference from all the other principles of all beings.

If one must also determine the proper principles for each of the mathematical sciences, what they are and of what sort, and what distinctive property they have in themselves, what difference from one another, and what difference from all the other principles of all beings, it is now time to go through these too. The best course of all is this: since there is a certain order among them, and some, as prior, take precedence not only in order but also in nature (for they abolish the others along with themselves but are not abolished along with them, and they bring the others in along with themselves but are not brought in along with them), while others fall short in both these respects, in seniority and simplicity, for these reasons it is fitting for us too to follow their natural order, and to speak first about the first, and then in turn about the others.

Of mathematical numbers, then, two principles must be posited as the very first and highest: the One (which indeed one ought not yet even to call a being, because it is simple and because it is a principle of beings, and the principle is not yet such as are those things of which it is the principle), and again another principle, that of multitude, which is able of itself to furnish division as well, and for this reason we would declare it, illustrating it as fittingly as we can, to be like a wholly fluid and pliant matter; and from these, the One and the principle of multitude, the first genus is brought to completion, numbers being composed from both of these with a certain persuasive necessity. And, going through each of the numbers one by one, one should say that it is this nature which furnishes all division to every number and, to speak generally, magnitude; whereas the fact that each of them is of a certain quality, and further determinate and one, is impressed by the undifferentiated and undivided principle setting its seal upon it. But it is perhaps not fitting to set down as evil or ugly a thing of this kind, to which it belongs to be of itself a cause of magnitude and division, and further of increase; for neither in other cases are we accustomed to place such a genus in the portion of evil, and there are times when we might perhaps truly say that the great, interwoven with a certain quality, is the cause of the magnificent and the liberal; so that it would be far from right to call it evil.

For if indeed one should happen to praise the nature of the One too for its self-sufficiency and for its being the cause of certain beautiful things among the numbers, how would it not be unreasonable to say that evil or the ugly is by nature receptive of such a thing? For it would then no longer turn out that evil and the ugly are in every way blameworthy, if indeed that which is receptive of something praiseworthy must itself too be called praiseworthy. Let this principle, then, be conceived by us in this way. The One, on the other hand, it is right to call neither beautiful nor good, because it is above both the beautiful and the good; for as nature proceeded further from the things at the beginning, first the beautiful appeared, and second, when the elements stand at a still greater distance, the good. The first receptacle and magnitude, then, or whatever one ought to call it, struck off the form of numbers, indeterminate in multitude, as is reasonable, but in some way determinate in form, having taken this over from the portion of the One. Now if one posits a single unlimited matter and receptacle for all things, it will in all likelihood turn out to be unreasonable that, when the form of the One comes to be in it, if indeed it is alike throughout, the same genera too should not be brought to completion once again. So the result will be that all the genera are altogether numbers; for we shall have no fitting difference to attach, to explain why ever a nature of numbers was generated here, and after this one of lines and planes and figures, and not always the same genus, coming as it does from elements that are alike and are interwoven with one another in the same manner.

But if someone posits the first cause of all multitude and magnitude as one, yet as furnishing many differences within itself, on account of which it is of a nature to bring forth ever different genera throughout the whole of nature, even though the One comes to be in it alike throughout, and yet not even this always displays its own nature exactly, owing to the grossness of the matter, like a shape in some chance pieces of wood, these consequences would perhaps follow for him not unreasonably; but that the first element should have divisions into so many differences is something at which one might perhaps fittingly take offence, especially if one were to carry the point right through in accordance with these examples; for what is simplest is everywhere an element. It remains, then, to posit some other cause of magnitude and, as in numbers the monad answers to the One, so to posit the point in lines; and position and the extension of places appear first in connection with lines and areas and solids, and in the same way place too makes its appearance here, owing to the fact that the difference of the receptacle hands on something proper to the genus that derives from it. Further, if one were to make this the cause of the continuous, and of what is more sullied and grosser than numbers, and say that they come from it, one would perhaps not go astray. And up to this point a second genus would have been brought to completion; for I place in the same genus lines and solids and the breadths of areas. First, then, is the matter of numbers, second that of lines and of plane and solid figures. And likewise for the other mathematical sciences, however many and of whatever kind reason may discover, their own receptacles must be presupposed.

Let this, then, stand so for us. The elements from which numbers come are not yet either beautiful or good; but from the composition of the One and the matter that is the cause of multitude number comes to exist, and it is in these first that being and beauty appear; next in order, from the elements of lines, geometrical essence appears, in which likewise there are being and the beautiful, and in these there is nothing either ugly or evil; but at the last, in the fourth and fifth things, those compounded from the last elements, evil arises, not in a primary way, but from certain things falling away from, and failing to keep hold of, what is according to nature.

From this it is evident also what difference the mathematical principles have from the others: for they stand out from the last principles because, while those are in some way corporeal, these are incorporeal; from those considered in respect of life because, while those are characterised by motion, these are unmoved; and from the intelligible principles because, while those pre-exist as indivisible, these furnish a principle of composition and division. Let the common account of the mathematical principles, and the account proper to each, be thus determined by us; and in what respect they differ from the other principles, let that be distinguished in this way.
Chapter 5
What things underlie all the mathematical sciences in common, with which lovers of learning are occupied in their study, and how it is possible to conduct the theory of them universally.

As for the things that underlie mathematical theory, those which extend in common over the whole of this science, they are all the theorems that are common, capable of applying to numbers, and capable also of applying to magnitudes, and further to harmonies and astronomy and all the rest.

Such are the theorems of proportions and those concerning compositions and divisions taken in common, and all that are studied concerning the equal and the unequal, in whatever condition or of whatever kind it may be, and all that examine the multiple or the divisible, or that which exceeds and that which falls short, or the determinate and the indeterminate by a common approach, or what is in itself and what is relative, or quantity simply, taking on in addition no particular species of quantity; and whatever studies the order and the beauty in the mathematical forms, in so far as these are scientific, without further specifying any particular kind of beauty (for a thing of that sort already touches upon the particular sciences); and again whatever considers the fixity and stability of mathematical science, which neither changes now in one way and now in another, nor departs from its own essence, nor is conceived now thus and afterwards otherwise: this too embraces by reasoning the common things that underlie mathematical science. One must not, however, suppose that these common things are supervenient, but that they exist prior to the particulars; nor that they have their essence in the particular things and together with them, but that they possess in advance an essence senior to those and more of the nature of a principle, one which does not, however, pervade them, but is ranked before the mathematical teachings proper to each science.

For this very reason the knowledge of them also is common and takes precedence, and is more perfect than the knowledge of the particulars: it forms a common synoptic view of them all; it orders all the mathematical theorems from one thing and towards one thing; it looks to their kinship and their likeness to one another, and observes alongside this what is unlike and other in them; it brings together into the same and distinguishes all their primary genera and species; it studies common agreed premises and first hypotheses and definitions and theses and divisions and collections, compositions and partitions, excesses and deficiencies and applications, in whatever genera of things having mathematical being, speaking simply and not determinately of each in particular; it discriminates the possible in these and the impossible, the necessary and the not necessary, the true and the false; and it searches out with exactness the differences in them, how many they are and of what kind.
Let so much be determined by us for the present, both concerning the things that underlie mathematical science in common and concerning the common mode of the theory that belongs to it.
Chapter 6
What the best use of the serious study of the mathematical sciences is, and to what end one ought to refer the best pursuit of them.

Concerning all such mathematical sciences this must be understood: that if someone grasps each of them rightly, great benefit comes to him who receives them in the proper manner; but if not, it is better always to call upon a god. The manner is this, for so much at least it is necessary to tell. Every diagram, and system of number, and every composition of harmony, and the proportion of the revolution of the stars, must be revealed to him who learns in the proper manner as being one for them all.

And it will be revealed, if someone learns rightly with his gaze fixed on what we are speaking of; for a single natural bond of all these things will be revealed to those who think it through. But if someone goes about it in some other way, he must call upon fortune, as indeed we say; for without these no nature will ever become happy in cities, but this is the way, this the nurture, these the mathematical sciences; whether they are hard or easy, by this road one must travel. And it is not lawful to neglect the gods, now that the auspicious report of them all, told in the proper manner, has become manifest. Him who has grasped all these things in this way, him I call most truly the wisest; for the fairest and most divine nature of all, as much of it as god has granted to human beings to behold, no one who has not beheld it will ever boast of having grasped it with ease apart from the things just now stated. In addition to these, one must bring to bear both what is taken one by one and what is taken by species in each of the kinds of knowledge that belong to the mathematical sciences, until we discover the whole cosmos, which reason, the most divine of all, has set in order as visible; which the happy man first marvelled at, and then conceived a passion to learn all that is possible for mortal nature, believing that thus he will pass his life in the best and most fortunate way, and that when he has died he will come to regions befitting virtue, and that, having been initiated truly and really, and having partaken, himself being one, of a wisdom that is one, he will continue for the rest of time as a spectator of the fairest things, as many as fall to sight.

One must also bring together the mathematical sciences that were pursued without order in the course of education into a synoptic view of the affinity of the mathematical sciences with one another and with the nature of being; for only learning of this kind is secure in those in whom it comes to be. One must also become able, letting go of the eyes and of the rest of sense-perception, to proceed in company with truth to being itself. One must also be steadfast in the mathematical sciences, and keen, and possessed of all the other qualities that befit the best nature; since, if we bring to so great a course of learning and so great a training people sound of limb and sound of mind, and so educate them, justice herself will find no fault with us, and we shall preserve both the city and the constitution; but if we lead to these things people of another sort, we shall bring about the opposite in everything and shall pour a still greater flood of ridicule over the love of learning. And if one must tell the whole truth as it stands, in these mathematical sciences a certain organ of each person’s soul is purified and rekindled, when it is being destroyed and blinded by the other pursuits, an organ more worth saving than ten thousand eyes; for by it alone is truth seen. To those, then, who share this view, the present remarks seem extraordinarily well said; but all who have in no way perceived this will reasonably think that we are saying nothing; for they see no other benefit from them worth speaking of.

But this, it seems, would be no spinning of a shell, but a turning round of the soul from a day that is a kind of night to the true day, which is an ascent to being, and which we shall indeed declare to be true love of learning. We must therefore consider which of the mathematical sciences has such a power, and which mathematical science is apt to draw the soul from what comes to be towards what is. I say, then, that among the things in our sense-perceptions some do not summon intellection to an examination, since they are adequately judged by sense-perception, while others in every way urge it to examine, since sense-perception produces nothing sound; and those that do not summon are all that do not pass over at the same time into an opposite sense-perception, while those that do pass over I set down as summoning, whenever sense-perception makes plain this thing no more than its opposite, whether it strikes us from close at hand or from afar. In the following way we shall know more clearly what I mean. These, we say, would be three fingers: the smallest, the second, and the middle one. Understand me, then, as speaking of them as seen from close at hand. But consider this point about them for me. Each of them, I suppose, appears equally a finger, and in this respect at least it makes no difference whether it is seen in the middle or at the end, whether it is white or black, whether thick or thin, and everything of that sort; for in all these cases the soul of most people is not compelled to ask intellection what a finger is; for nowhere did sight itself indicate at the same time that the finger is the opposite of a finger.

Reasonably, then, a thing of this sort would not be apt to summon intellection. But what of this? Does sight see their largeness and their smallness adequately, and does it make no difference to it whether one of them lies in the middle or at the end? And likewise touch, with thickness and thinness and hardness? And will not the other senses reveal such things defectively? Or does each of them act as follows: first, the sense that is set over the hard is compelled to be set over the soft as well, and reports to the soul that it perceives the same thing as both hard and soft? Necessarily, then, in such cases the soul in its turn is at a loss as to what the sense itself means by the hard, if indeed it says that the same thing is also soft, and as to what the sense of the light and that of the heavy mean by the light and heavy, if it indicates that the heavy is light and the light heavy; for these communications are strange to the soul and in need of examination. Reasonably, then, in such cases the soul first of all, summoning reasoning and intellection, tries to examine whether each of the things reported to it is one or two. Now if they appear to be two, each of the two appears as other and as one; if, then, each is one and both together are two, it will conceive the two as separated; for it would not conceive things unseparated as two, but as one.

Sight too, certainly, saw large and small, as we say, yet not as separated but as something confused together; and for the sake of clarity about this, intellection in its turn was compelled to see large and small, not confused together but distinguished, in the opposite way to sight. So it is from some such point as this that it first occurs to us to ask: what, then, will the large be, and again the small? And so it was that we called the one intelligible and the other visible. This, then, is what I was attempting to say just now, that some things are apt to summon discursive thought and others are not, defining as apt to summon it those that fall upon sense-perception together with their own opposites, and those that do not as not apt to rouse intellection. What then? To which of the two classes number and the one and the other objects of mathematical study seem to belong, it is easy to reckon from what has been said before. For if the one, or any other of the objects of mathematical study, is itself adequately seen or grasped by some other sense, it would not be apt to draw us towards essence, just as we were saying in the case of the finger; but if some contrariety is always seen together with it, so that it appears no more one than the opposite as well, there would at once be need of something to adjudicate, and the soul would be compelled in this case to be at a loss and to inquire, setting in motion the thought within itself, and to ask what the one itself is; and thus the study of the one would be among those that lead and turn one round to the vision of being. But surely the sight of it possesses this feature not least of all; for we see the same thing at once as one and as unlimited in multitude. So then, if this is true of the one, all number too is affected in the same way as it. But surely calculation and arithmetic are wholly concerned with number; and these evidently lead towards truth; pre-eminently, then, as it seems, this would be among the mathematical sciences we are seeking.

And the others too would in the same way be useful for science, because they lay hold of essence and are set free from becoming, and summon intellection while withdrawing us from the senses, and summon us to the vision of the nature of the things that are, and furnish the soul itself with ease in its turning round from becoming to truth and essence. One must also pursue the mathematical sciences for the sake of knowing; for in this way the soul is led powerfully somewhere upwards, and they compel people to discourse about the things themselves that are, never accepting it if someone, in discoursing with them, puts forward visible or tangible bodies; for they speak of those things which it is possible only to grasp in thought, and which it is impossible to handle in any other way. The mathematical sciences, then, are likely to be necessary, since they evidently compel the soul to employ intellection itself in pursuit of truth itself; and moreover they make people become keener than they were, and further they afford much toil to one who learns and practises them.

One must also consider whether they tend in any way towards that, namely towards making it easier to behold the Idea of the Good. And all things tend that way, we say, which compel the soul to turn round to that region in which is the happiest part of being, which the soul must by every means see. So then, if a thing compels us to contemplate essence, it is fitting; if becoming, it is not fitting. And those that are pursued for the sake of knowledge are to be honoured as being mathematical sciences: all that lay hold of knowledge of what always is, and not of what at some time comes to be and perishes.

These, then, would be apt to draw the soul towards truth, and productive of philosophic thought, so as to direct upwards what we now wrongly keep turned downwards; for by these alone is truth seen. They must therefore be inquired into continuously and strenuously, so that it may become manifest how they stand. For in addition to everything else they also possess charm in an exceptional degree, and make the soul look upwards. Of this kind are those mathematical sciences that are concerned with being and the invisible, and all that are to be grasped by reason and discursive thought, but not by sight. One should indeed use the things that appear as models; one ought not, however, to examine them in earnest as though one were going to grasp in them the truth of equals or doubles or any other commensurability. For it is indeed absurd if someone should suppose that these things come about always in the same way and never deviate in any respect at all, though they have bodies and are visible, and should seek by every means to grasp the truth of them. Throughout all this one must guard against the following: that those whom we shall educate should ever attempt to learn any of these things in an incomplete form, one that does not in every case come out at the point at which all things ought to arrive; for in this way they will be useful for the search for the beautiful and good, but pursued otherwise they are useless. And I think, too, that if the methodical inquiry into all these mathematical sciences arrives at their communion and kinship with one another, and they are reckoned together in the respect in which they are akin to one another, the pursuit of them contributes to what we want and the labour is not unprofitable; but if not, it is unprofitable.

For the release from the bonds and the turning round from the shadows to the images and the light, and the ascent from the underground and sensible realm to the sun and the Good, and there the continuing inability to look upon the animals and the plants and the light of the sun, that is, upon the pure forms and genera, but the ability to look upon the divine appearances in water and the shadows of the things that are, and not shadows of images cast by another light which, judged in relation to the sun, is itself of the same sort: all this pursuit of the arts which we have gone through has this power, and effects a leading up of what is best in the soul to the vision of what is most excellent among the things that are, just as then what is clearest in the body was led to the vision of what is brightest in the bodily and visible region. Of some such kind is the best use of the mathematical sciences, and such is their most sovereign end.
Chapter 7

What object of science proper to it underlies each mathematical science, and how it is possible to make the common distinction of them on the basis of division, so as to know what sort of thing the one and the multitude in the mathematical sciences is, and how one ought to define it.

Since we must also determine, for each mathematical science, the proper object of science that underlies it, come, let us begin from division and distinguish the species of the objects of mathematical study with which they deal. For in this way we should most easily learn of what sort the one and the multitude of mathematical science is, and by what differences it is distinguished. Let us begin from the following point.

The whole nature of the continuous and of the discrete is conceived along with beings, that is, with the constitution of the whole cosmos, in two ways: that of the discrete by juxtaposition and heaping together, that of the continuous by unification and mutual coherence.

In the strict sense, what is continuous and unified would be called magnitude, and what is juxtaposed and discrete, multitude. And according to the essence of magnitude the cosmos would be conceived and spoken of as one, and as solid and spherical, grown together with itself, extended and held together in mutual coherence; while according to the form and notion of multitude, in turn, there would be conceived the arrangement and ordering and harmony of the universe, having its constitution from, let us say, so many elements and spheres and stars and genera and animals and plants, and oppositions and likenesses. But of what is unified the cutting proceeds in every case without limit, while its increase proceeds to a determinate point; whereas of multitude, by a reciprocal relation, the increase proceeds without limit, while the cutting, conversely, proceeds to a determinate point, both being by nature and in conception unlimited, and on that account not to be circumscribed by sciences; ‘for there will not even be anything that is going to know at all, if all things are unlimited’, as Philolaus says. But since it is necessary that the nature of science be discerned in beings that have been so exactly wrought by divine providence, certain sciences, cutting off a portion of each and setting a limit to what they had embraced, called what was taken from multitude quantity, which is at once knowable, and in the same way what was taken from magnitude size.

And they brought both of these genera under sciences, the kinds of knowledge proper to them: quantity under arithmetic, size under geometry. But since these were not of a single form, and each of them admitted a still more particular subdivision (for of quantity one part was quantity by itself, freed from any relation to another, as for example even, odd, perfect, deficient and the like, while the other was quantity standing in some relation to something else, which is properly called relative quantity, as for example equal, unequal, multiple, superparticular, superpartient and the like; and again, of size one part exists and is conceived as at rest, the other as in motion and borne along), for this reason, reasonably enough, two other sciences came to share with the two already brought in and joined them in laying hold of the study of each object of science. For arithmetic, which received as its proper lot the inquiry into quantity by itself, was joined by music, which took as its share the systematic treatment of relative quantity (for its harmonic part and its part concerning concords profess nothing other than to articulate the relations and ratios of the notes to one another and the quantity of their excesses and deficiencies); while geometry, occupied with the examination of size that is at rest and stationary, found a helper in spherics, which was established as the judge of size in motion, that is, of the most perfect size, the one that has received an ordered and uniform motion.

Wherefore, since these sciences too have come to be concerned with underlying objects that are sisters, it is reasonable to consider the sciences themselves sisters as well, so that the saying of Archytas may not go unheeded, ‘for these mathematical sciences seem to be sisters’, and to hold that they cling to one another in the manner of the links of a chain and end in a single bond, as the most divine Plato says, and that the kinship of these mathematical sciences ought to be revealed as one to him who learns in the proper manner; and him who has grasped all these things in this way, as he himself lays it down, he calls most truly the wisest, and he strongly affirms it in play, and he enjoins upon those who are eager to philosophise that these mathematical sciences are to be pursued and chosen at all costs, whether they be hard or easy; and very reasonably so, if indeed apprehensions of the continuous and the discrete come about through these alone, and the cosmos and all the things in it are composed of the continuous and the discrete.

Now the exact apprehension of these is wisdom, the desire for wisdom is philosophy, and philosophy, alone among all arts and sciences, secures for man the end that is proper and natural to him and leads to the happiness which, in distinction from the other animals, belongs to him alone and which is by nature earnestly pursued as the end most fit to be his aim.
Chapter 8
What the common criterion of all the mathematical sciences is, and how it is discovered from the section of the line which the Pythagoreans hand down.

Next after this we must speak also of the criterion of all the mathematical sciences, what sort of thing it is and what differences of activities it has within itself. Taking the matter up from the beginning, then, let us conduct the whole of our instruction about it on the basis of division.

All intelligibles, then, are divided into two: into those called intelligibles in the proper sense and objects of science, and into the objects of discursive thought; and the intelligibles are first, while the objects of discursive thought are second and inferior. Again, after these there is another essence, that of sensibles, and of these some are sensibles in the proper sense, which are also objects of opinion, while the others are objects of conjecture. Objects of opinion and sensibles in the proper sense are the particular bodies, such as stones, pieces of wood, the four elements, and these are first among sensibles; after them come others that are weak and not like them, but are consequent upon the first. These are shadows; for shadows are concomitants of bodies, and if they did not have some other body lying beneath them, they would not appear. Shadows, then, and the things in waters and in mirrors are images, existing in other things and not by themselves, nor appearing apart from other things, but having fallen upon other bodies, and when these are withdrawn they do not appear.

Hence they are sensibles in genus, because they fall under sense-perception, but they are objects of conjecture and of belief rather than things having real existence, being so called in accordance with the belief that attaches to things which are not demonstrative but are otherwise taken up for acceptance, out of belief in those who put them forward. For shadows do not have from themselves that which makes for apprehension, but from the bodies upon which they have fallen and in which, coming to rest, they appear. Such belief, then, is unstable; for if these things were to depart from the mirror or the water or the ground, they would be nothing at all. So that, whereas even bodies are objects of opinion and possess their being in seeming, shadows rank still lower, in that they do not have solidity from themselves but rest upon something else. Now the objects of discursive thought too resemble these, standing to the objects of science and the intelligibles in the same ratio as objects of conjecture to sensibles and objects of opinion. For the intellect holds the Ideas, which are the things that truly are, as it were by contact, whereas the objects of discursive thought, which are the geometrical objects, are beheld by discursive thought, discursive thought no longer drawing near to them directly and as it were by immediate apprehension, but its approach to them coming about rather through reason, and as though we were descending from the Ideas to likenesses of them and intelligible images.

And likewise the objects of conjecture, those in shadows, rank below sensibles, in that the latter fall under sense-perception by themselves and in a direct line, while the former are observed in another, upon another and on account of another. For the shadow certainly does not exist by itself, but either on the ground, which is sensible by itself, or in the mirror or in the waters, which were, as we saw, sensible by themselves. In this way, then, mathematical objects too seem to appear as it were in the Ideas, and to have their support upon them; for they must not be conceived by abstraction from sensibles, but as having descended from the Ideas and having their character as images from them, by having taken on magnitude in addition and by appearing in extension. For what faintness and want of any support in itself are in the images of sensibles, that bulk and extension are in the intelligible ones; but since this too hastens towards what is without bulk and without parts, it seems to come to rest in the partlessness of the Ideas, as shadows do in the resistance of sensibles. Just as the objects of discursive thought, then, are separated from the intelligibles, so too is discursive thought from intellection. That is why Brotinus too, in his On Intellect and Discursive Thought, separating them from one another, says the following: ‘Discursive thought is greater than intellect, and the object of discursive thought than the intelligible; for intellect is that which is simple and incomposite and which primarily thinks and is thought (and such is the form; for it is without parts and incomposite and prior to the others), whereas discursive thought is that which is manifold and divisible and which thinks secondarily (for it has taken on science and reason in addition), and similarly too the objects of discursive thought; and these are the objects of science and the demonstrables and the universals, which are grasped by intellect through reason.’

In these words he calls discursive thought and the object of discursive thought greater, not in power but in multitude (and these stand in inverse relation to one another), and he marks them off from intellect and the intelligibles not by these alone, but also by the fact that the one set are simple and incomposite, the other multiform and composite; and because the one set think and are thought primarily, the other secondarily and as receiving from the former the activity of doing so; and the one set are established in forms, while the other exercise a manifold activity in reasonings; and the one are indivisible, the other divisible; and the one are superior to demonstrative syllogism, while the other reason syllogistically to some conclusion about beings; and the one are the beings themselves, while the other have embraced the particulars in the universals and display them along with these; and the one employ immaterial and pure activities, while the other have their intellection mixed; for they grasp the objects of knowledge proper to them by intellect through reason, or by intellect together with reason. It follows from this, then, that both the things judged and their criteria stand apart from one another, so that the objects of discursive thought differ from the intelligibles, and discursive thought from intellect.
Still more clearly does Archytas, in his On Intellect and Sense-Perception, distinguish the criteria of beings, and he sets forth the criterion most proper to mathematical objects in these words:

‘For in ourselves’, he says, ‘there are, in respect of the soul, four kinds of cognition: intellect, science, opinion, sense-perception; of which two are principles of reason, namely intellect and sense-perception, and two are its ends, namely science and opinion; and like is always capable of knowing like. It is clear, then, that intellect in us is capable of knowing the intelligibles, science the objects of science, opinion the objects of opinion, and sense-perception the sensibles; for which reason, then, discursive thought must pass over from the sensibles to the objects of opinion, from the objects of opinion to the objects of science, and from these to the intelligibles; and these are to be brought into concord, and when contemplated through themselves they are true. With these things determined, we must consider what comes next. For just as a line is cut in two, and again equal segments of each part are cut in the same ratio, so too let the intelligible be divided in relation to the visible, and again let each be marked off in the same way, and let them differ in clarity and obscurity relative to the others. In the same way, then, of the sensible one segment is the images in waters and in mirrors, and the other part is the things of which these are likenesses, plants and animals; and of the intelligible the part that stands analogously, as the likenesses do, is the genera with which the mathematical sciences are concerned.

For those who are concerned with geometry, having hypothesised the odd and the even and figures and three species of angles, work out the rest from these, but leave the things themselves alone as though they knew them, and are unable to give an account of them either to themselves or to others; rather, they make use of sensibles, as is natural, yet it is not these that they are inquiring into, nor is it for the sake of these that they construct their arguments, but for the sake of the diagonal and of the square itself. The other segment of the intelligible is that with which dialectic is occupied; for dialectic itself treats the hypotheses as really hypotheses, but as starting-points and stepping-stones, in order that it may come as far as the unhypothetical, to the principle of everything, and, keeping hold, may descend again to the conclusion, making no additional use of anything sensible, but of forms themselves through themselves. And to these four segments it is well to distribute also the affections of the soul, and to call the one at the highest intellection, the one at the second discursive thought, the one at the third belief, and the one at the fourth conjecture.’

I think, then, that through these words too it has become quite plain that there are four differences among beings and four principles of judgement, and that reason, holding a middle position, lays hold of the two extremes, the intelligibles and the sensibles, being set in the rank of an end in relation to intellect and sense-perception, since these are its principles, and being brought to completion by them.

This too is a common axiom concerning every cognitive faculty, that like things are known by like. It is possible, then, to learn both from both, and the one set of these from the other, and possible to make the equal divisions in their case both in common and in particular, and an order of transition from the one set to the other, that is, from the inferior to the higher; and he has determined how one must effect the ascent and co-ordination of all things towards intellect. Next after this he cuts the line, which is one, in order that we may conceive of the cognitive faculty as one, but he divides it in two in accordance with the primary differences among beings and the judgements, divided in two, that bear upon them. And he posits these divisions as equal in virtue of their participation in the reason-principles and the forms, and on account of the likeness of the things that participate to the things participated in, and because the proportion is in a way the same in both. Again, he divides each of the segments in the same ratio, since the cognitive faculty is throughout of the same form as itself, and he makes its differences lie in clarity and obscurity and in being perfectly or deficiently determined, and he exhibits their distinction from one another, showing in what respect the second deviate from and are inferior to the prior. First he divides the sensible, as being more familiar, and takes from it the existence that appears, by way of likeness, from the sensibles, namely the images in waters and in mirrors, cutting it off as a single nature.

The other part he marks off as the true one, the things of which these are likenesses, such as plants and animals. For it is from these that conjecture of the images arises, sense-perception being turned towards the latter by reflection and so knowing them secondarily, just as they also exist in a secondary manner, whereas it applies itself to the sensibles immediately, just as they also exist primarily and have their enmattered existence in themselves. From the proportion of these, then, it is possible to understand the other segment as well. For the genera with which the mathematical sciences are concerned are analogous to the likenesses, and the cognitions of them have a certain likeness to the conjectures of the images; for they receive their activity from intellections and pass over from the intelligibles to mathematical objects as to likenesses, and they make use of hypotheses and do not know the cause. And this is the criterion of mathematical objects, being a faculty of prior knowledge of a different thing, and not of the intelligible, and apprehending the object of discursive thought by a different cognition, and not by intellection; for intellection is the criterion of the dialectician, and through it he contemplates beings and the forms and all things unhypothetical, and is able to give an account of all things, and makes no additional use of anything sensible, but of the intelligible forms. Since, then, the judging faculties are four, a certain order among them is observed and their activities are in fact divided: at the highest intellection, at the second discursive thought, at the third belief, and conjecture at the fourth.
From these considerations, then, on the basis of division, it has been sufficiently shown what the criterion of the mathematical sciences is.
Chapter 9

On those who assign a determinate essence to the mathematical sciences, of whom the first opinion set out is that of those who refer it to soul; several reasons for such a hypothesis are stated, and starting-points for the whole theory concerning them.

But if we must now go on to grasp in a determinate way as well the form of mathematics, both what it is and how it subsists, let us look first at the opinion of those who refer it to soul; for upon this one could fix one’s thought in a determinate way.

Now one would not reasonably posit the soul as one single genus among the things that exist in the mathematical sciences, on such an approach to the theory; for in that way the knowledge of mathematical essence would become divided. Hence one should not define it separately as the form of what is extended in every direction, or as a self-moved number, or as a harmony subsisting in ratios, or as anything else of that kind; rather it is right to weave them all together in common, on the ground that the soul is both a numerical form and subsists in accordance with numbers that embrace a harmony; and all the commensurabilities in common, as many as fall under mathematics, are to be ranked under it, and the proportions as a whole are to be placed under it. For this reason, then, it coexists with geometrical, arithmetical and harmonic proportion all together, whence indeed it is also identical with the ratios that accord with proportion, has a certain kinship with the principles of beings, lays hold of all beings, and is able to be made like to all things.

Such, then, are the reasons for this sort of supposition. But starting-points for the theory, the mathematical and that concerning the soul together, would arise if we were to observe that everything limited and determinate reaches it from numbers, and the unitary reason-principle from the nature of the One, while the power that proceeds to magnitude and increase and has abundance, so as to give itself to all things of due measure, is present to it from geometrical essence; and the power of harmonious motion, and order, and the commensurability of things irrational, and the good measure found in numbers that are concordant or embrace concord, come to it from essential harmony. That is why the soul both hearkens to harmonies and delights in things attuned, as being itself too a harmony, and has its essence from numbers and other such mathematical measures, which have received a kinship both with the intelligible forms and with sensible essences and the enmattered forms; for the present opinion gives a starting-point for theory in relation to all of these, since the mathematical opinion thus hypothesised is sufficient to furnish all such conceptions. To sum up the whole opinion: we conceive the soul as existing in reason-principles common to all the mathematical sciences, possessing on the one hand the capacity to judge them, and possessing on the other the capacity to generate and produce the incorporeal measures themselves, to which one can also fit the generative production of the enmattered forms and the fashioning by means of images, which proceeds from the unseen into the manifest and joins what is outside to what is within.
For in all these respects, to put it comprehensively, the reason-principle of the soul contains of itself the entire complement of the mathematical sciences.
Chapter 10

How the essence of the soul is constituted out of all the mathematical sciences, and by what determination their blending in it might be defined, and whether it contains in itself the whole existence of the mathematical sciences or some other principle of them is also observed.

But whether it is a mixture of all the things that exist in the mathematical sciences, or itself brings them all into existence in virtue of a single antecedent reason-principle, must be examined. If, then, it is a commixture from them all, the things that make it up, from whose coming together it is blended, exist before it, and it would no longer itself be the principle of mathematical essence; rather, since it is generated from mathematical sciences that subsist in scattered fashion and come together into the same thing, this, besides the other absurdities, also brings in along with the soul a kind of composition and an existence that is later-born, as arising subsequently out of certain prior things. If, however, it is itself primarily the originator of mathematical essence and brings this forth out of itself, it will be senior to it, and it both precedes it as holding the rank of cause and is superior as being other than it. But this too is contrary to the present opinion; for in that way the soul would turn out to be more honourable than the things that exist in the mathematical sciences. It is better, then, to say that it neither precedes nor follows upon the things that exist mathematically, but runs together with them simultaneously and subsists along with them, having its commixture in them all and from them all as something incomposite and indivisible, being present to them in a uniform manner and participating in them all in a unitary manner, having gathered into itself a power that embraces them all and having given itself in the same way to all the mathematical sciences.

And if this is so, it has also embraced all things in itself perfectly and without deficiency, and leaves nothing outside itself (for it is itself perfect, and it is not possible for any of the things that are to be left without its own principle), and in this way the essence will be one, since the same principle extends through them all. Differences, however, there will be none the less, in accordance with the different powers, lives and activities of the soul and the multitude of its essences, which is contained in one. Such is the determination that one might reasonably lay down concerning these matters too.
Let so much, then, be said by us concerning the essence of mathematical theory.
Chapter 11
What the work of mathematical theory is and how it comes about, and that it is named ‘mathematical’ in agreement with these things.

The work of this science is not determinate, nor is it in the same condition and in the same way, like that of intellect, nor does it altogether have its knowing from itself, as that sort of thing is connate with intellect; rather it is roused from outside towards its cognitions, and, receiving from others the starting-point of recollection, it thus projects it from itself; nor is it stable in a single activity, like that of intellect, but rather proceeds in motion from itself and to itself. Nor yet is it full of itself, like what is intellective, but in seeking and finding it always advances from a certain emptiness of knowing to the filling of itself. And it is likewise held in the middle between limit and unlimitedness; whence it always advances from the unlimited towards being determined, and passes over to partaking of the mathematical forms.

It is for all these reasons, then, that this science comes about with learning first leading the way, the starting-point of which is supplied by the teacher, and discovery then following, which is attached to the starting-points laid down by the teacher; for it is in accordance with these that the soul recollects the true forms in mathematics and projects the reason-principles proper to them. Sometimes, however, the activity also comes to be a common one, arising from both, which is why Archytas in his On Mathematics says: ‘For you must come to know the things of which you were ignorant either by learning from another or by discovering them yourself. Now learning is from another and by another’s means, while discovering is through oneself and one’s own; and to discover without seeking is difficult and rare, but with seeking it is accessible and easy, whereas for one who does not know, to seek is impossible.’ For in these words he put learning first, as the starting-point of this kind of science, and pointed out what is proper to it, namely that it is imparted by another. Second he added ‘discovering them yourself’; for even if this takes precedence in power, still in the human order at least, relative to us, it is second; for those who have fallen into generation must first be reminded by others. Now it is possible to take these as two ways of receiving science, but it is also possible to comprehend them in reasoning as one; for whenever we have acquired the mathematical sciences as from another and as belonging to another, we then bring them to hand ourselves from ourselves as our own.

This is easy to learn from discoveries; for it is as having them in ourselves that we discover them, and recognise them once they are discovered. The same thing is evident from acts of seeking as well. For if it is impossible for one who does not know to seek, there was a time when we knew these things, and it is not this present time (for now we are ignorant of them); therefore we knew them previously. And for this reason the mathematical sciences are accessible and easy to discover for one who seeks, but difficult and rare for one who does not seek, because they are in a way present in souls, and at some earlier time were with them in scientific knowledge that was in activity. The study that proceeds by way of the mathematical sciences, then, is a road from seeking to discovery, and from learning to seeking and discovery. Hence indeed it has also got this name, that of being called mathematical (mathēmatikē). For from that from which the science first receives its starting-point and without which it cannot arise in us, I mean learning (manthanein), from this it has taken its name.
Let these points too about it, then, stand as thus clarified by us.
Chapter 12
What the powers of mathematical science are, what orders they have among themselves, according to how many differences they are divided, and in how many ways they are conceived.

As for its powers, one might enumerate many others besides, but among the first let there be considered those that gather from multitude towards the cause that is the same and unified, and all those that divide from the one into multitude.

For since they are constituted out of limit and unlimitedness and out of the One and multitude, and are intermediate between the divisible and the indivisible, they have also, in accordance with the same account of their essence, a share in both gathering and division, in both unfolding and rolling together, and in both reversion to the determinate and departure from it. Now this sort of activity of contemplation is found in dialectic too, which is concerned primarily with being; nevertheless this science does differ from that one in no small respect: for the one contemplates being without qualification, and gathers or divides this, whereas the other examines mathematical being and exercises these twofold activities of reason upon it. There are also other powers which look to what is common over many things, all those that contemplate in the differing mathematical sciences certain common forms and common ratios and common measures by which the things that differ are marked off, such as the studies of equality and inequality and those of the commensurable and incommensurable; for these powers contemplate what subsists in common over several things. Opposed to these are those that contemplate what is proper to the essence of each thing, for instance of numbers in so far as they are numbers, and of magnitudes in so far as they subsist as magnitudes, and in the same way in the other cases. Among such powers are also those that apprehend the proportion that subsists everywhere, beginning from above with the very first things, ending at the last, proceeding through the intermediates, and everywhere preserving the same ratios, and different ones in things that differ, and rendering them manifest throughout the whole. Moreover, those that contemplate the beauty and the measure of mathematical essences, and what is attuned and commensurate in them, must also be held of some account; for they have by their own proper nature good order and perfection and all the goods that befit mathematical forms.

Now to most people these powers seem both to be unmoved themselves and to be active about objects of knowledge that are unmoved; but this view is not correct. For there are certain mathematical sciences which examine the number of motion and its measures, how they stand both in themselves and in relation to one another in point of order and commensurability, and the incorporeal revolutions of the soul, with which the circuits of the heaven also coexist, how they stand in point of commensurability and according to what numbers, and why they fit together, and which examine all such matters; among these, indeed, astronomy and harmonics are included. In order, then, that the mathematical powers may extend also to those that contemplate motions, these too must be posited as contained under mathematical science. Over against these one must distinguish the stable powers, which contemplate the unmoved forms and ratios and are able to reckon out the order of these relative to one another; among them are the majority of the powers connate with mathematics. Their orders must be marked off according to the essence of the objects of knowledge which they contemplate, whether some take precedence and others are subordinate, and according to the ranking in honour of the beautiful, whether some contemplate the most senior and highest beauty and others that which is inferior and imperfect. The differences among them are to be taken from the manner of their activities and the variation in their knowledge, and from the different beings that are yoked with them, with which they interweave their acts of learning.

The question in how many ways they are conceived must be examined from the varied objects of knowledge that learning has; for from these the powers are seen both to subsist themselves in many ways and to exercise their activities in manifold fashion.

In this way one might mark these things out at the beginning, as in an outline. But, as is fitting, one must await the full account of them; for in that way above all the teaching about them would be handed down complete.
Chapter 13

What the elements and genera of mathematical science are, and in what way the same things are elements and in what way genera, and in what respect these differ from those in the other sciences and essences, both the intelligible ones and all that are in generation.

Since every theory and every science derives its unshakeable character from its first elements, when these are determinate and never otherwise, and attains its most perfect comprehension from the passage through the elements, and since, further, each finds from its own proper genera the manner of arguments and demonstrations appropriate to itself, it is necessary in the case of mathematics too both to distinguish beforehand those elements of it that are most common to the whole concerted effort of the mathematical sciences, and to hunt for the genera that are most proper to it and that most of all extend in common to everything. And when we have discerned these, let us consider in turn whether the elements will be one thing and the genera another, or whether the same things are viewed in one way as genera and in another as elements, and in what respect such things in mathematics differ from the genera and elements in the other sciences and essences, both all that are intelligible and all that are borne along in generation.

That the elements and genera of mathematics are determinate and always at rest is both agreed by the best of those engaged in philosophy and clearly attested by the mathematical demonstrations themselves, which are always in the same condition and in the same way.

And that the account of these also agrees with the first principles of mathematical essence is easy to learn; for here too the One and multitude, limit and the unlimited, sameness and otherness, are elements and genera of the science and of the things known by it. Whenever, then, we consider these as causes and as productive of the whole of mathematical essence and of the theory concerning it, let the causes just mentioned be conceived as principles; whenever they are conceived as inherent and as completing the essence and the account of the science, let them be conceived as elements; and whenever we discern them as common, holding of all the mathematical sciences, furnishing the bond of essence for the particular ones and none the less subsisting themselves by themselves, then let us view them as genera. The same things, therefore, are in one way originative of mathematical theory and of the things known by it as beings, in another way are conceived as elements, and in yet another way again as genera; not because they differ conceptually, in account alone, nor because they change along with their different relations and turn from one thing into another, but because the same things make several processions and differences within themselves. And indeed, what is without difference is also disposed in accordance with the difference of cause; for it is not the same thing for one of the incorporeals to be by itself and to be completive of other things, nor again have that which is productive of certain things and that which contributes in any way whatever to essence obtained the same rank.

Nor is there any way in which that which is co-ordinated with other things ever ranks the essence it has by itself in that co-ordination; rather, it leaves that essence apart, and weaves the other into the completion of those essences to whose being it contributes. By the same reasoning, then, the cause that furnishes being does not coexist with the things brought to completion by it either, but is senior to them in the very account of its essence, and has in itself a separate existence, on account of which it also gives to the things torn asunder by it another existence, after itself. In this way, then, the unlimited and limit have been reasonably marked off by us among principles and elements and genera alike. These differ from the intelligible principles, elements and genera in that they fall short of them in perfection and purity and simplicity, and in the comprehensiveness that extends furthest, in being determinate, and further in beauty and in all goods; while they surpass those in generation in order, in commensurability, in their unmoved and stable nature, in their pure participation in forms, in their incorporeal and immaterial nature, and, to speak comprehensively, in all the better attributes. From this, then, it is inferred that they are intermediate between both of these, and hold a middle rank that is able to have communion with both and to ferry across to both of them equally.
One who came to such determinations about these matters too would not miss what is fitting.
Chapter 14

On mathematical likeness and unlikeness: what they are, how far they extend, and how they are present in mathematical essence; and in what respect they differ from the genera of the same name that are spoken of among intelligibles and among sensibles.

As for likeness and unlikeness, everyone would agree that there is a great deal of it in the mathematical sciences and in mathematical essence, and that it has great power there; for it is not even possible to know any theorem mathematically unless one constructs it by defining some figure like it, conducting the argument about it by means of another image, and constructing one thing from another according to a single account, that of likeness.

But what deserves study is this: what these common features of the like and the unlike are, how far they extend in the mathematical sciences, how they are present in them, and in what respect they differ from the things homonymously called like and unlike among intelligibles or sensibles. Now this must be understood: that in the case of mathematical essence the like and the unlike are not spoken of in respect of quality, nor in respect of figure of the kind that supervenes in certain cases as one thing upon others; for qualities of that sort tend to occur in composite things and in connection with composition, where the substrate is one thing and the accident in the substrate another, working a character and a specific form into the underlying nature; whereas the like and unlike that we are now investigating is senior to all composition. Nor again is it viewed in terms of a relation of the kind that subsists in being disposed in a certain way; for one must not conceive the existences of things that exist by themselves as depending on other things. Let it be laid down, then, that the like and unlike now under discussion holds primarily in respect of essence, not every essence, however, but mathematical essence. These, then, will be certain forms of mathematical essence. For one ought not to set quality and quantity in a division over against essence, and then assign one theoretical science to essence and another to quantity, and mark off this latter as being mathematical science; rather, just as its nature is, so too one should examine the proper mathematical essence, and these forms, how many they are and of what kind; and the quantity which the science does also examine along with it is neither the quantity in bodies nor the intelligible paradigm, but so much as is mathematical; in the same way, then, it is naturally fitted to consider along with it the like and the unlike too, whether as common genera or species concerning the essence, or as common powers generative of the forms in the particular mathematical sciences, according to the very account of being.

They extend, in the case of mathematical essence as a whole, to the whole of its being, and in the case of the particular mathematical sciences, to their divided existences; and thus, to whatever extent one considers more or fewer, greater or lesser circumscriptions of these, the like and the unlike are coextensive with them all, reaching either further or less far. For it is altogether impossible for multitude or division or unification or sameness and otherness to exist among genuinely mathematical objects unless essential likeness and unlikeness have gone before. Let us no longer wonder, then, that they extend to one genus and to more and to fewer and to all; far rather ought we to consider this, that they are present in each in a manner akin to it, according to the proper character of each. And this too must be considered, I mean the one and the many of the like and the unlike and what lies between these, and one must look to what their fitting order is, and to their distribution among each of the mathematical sciences, according as each of these is naturally fitted to partake of them.

If this is so, then that mathematical science would be the most authoritative of all which discovers the same cause of likeness and of unlikeness alike in prior and in posterior things, and, in the case of things of the same rank, makes the due distinction between them. How, then, each of them comes to be present we should best understand if here too we were to preserve the peculiar character of the essence that is the subject of our account. In the same way what is common in them too is unalloyed and uncorrupted. Since, then, we are agreed on these points, we must also grasp this: that mathematical likeness and unlikeness ought to be taken as different from the likeness and unlikeness found among intelligibles and from that found among sensibles.

It will be distinguished from them in one way, that by which we distinguished the three essences (for it is clear that, since these differ in three ways, the forms in them too will differ in three ways), and in another way, because it is delimited by its intermediate nature between them, those being extremes and marking off the beginning and the end of the forms that concern their own essence; and in yet another way, let some be conceived as originative, others as arising in the rank of an effect, and others as growing up between the causes that lead and the things brought to completion as last. Having grasped these points in advance, we should easily be able, starting from them, to study in due order also the like and unlike things proper to each of the mathematical sciences, whenever we give the account proper to them; for the present, let what is common concerning them be taken as stated by us thus far.

Constituted, then, from genera, principles and elements of such a kind and so many, and being such as we have already described it, mathematical science does not extend only a short way, nor to a mere few of the affairs of life, but contributes to the greatest and finest of goods, both divine and human.

Moreover, the proper modes of the Pythagorean transmission of the mathematical sciences possessed a wonderful exactness, and differed greatly from the technical instruction given by those who spend their time on the mathematical sciences. Further, and following upon this, they made it their practice to exhibit first the discoveries of the theorems, and to use nothing as though it were already given, but in every case to consider how that which is proved in the mathematical sciences might come into existence. There was also another mode among them, the mathematical mode through symbols, as for instance the pentad is the symbol of justice, because it signifies symbolically all the species of what is just.

This form was useful to them for the whole of philosophy, since they taught most things symbolically, and held this mode to be proper to the gods and suited to nature. But that they did also hand down the first principles and the discoveries of the mathematical sciences is clear from the other mathematical sciences as well, and is manifest also from the arithmetical methods. For they teach thoroughly how each genus and species of numbers is primarily generated and how it is discovered by us, on the ground that the study of these things is not scientific unless one grasps them by starting from above.
