And they made the references of the mathematical sciences to the things that are either by a sharing in the same ratios, or by some faint reflection, or by a likeness, whether closely approaching or standing far off, or by a certain representation in images, or by an antecedent cause, as in a paradigm, or in some other way. And in other ways too, of many kinds, they yoke the mathematical sciences to things, on the ground that things are able to be made like the mathematical sciences, and the mathematical sciences are of a nature to be likened to things, and both are reciprocally assimilated to one another.

In variety of argument, then, and in abundance of methods they took no very great delight, regarding this as too much a matter of mere reasoning and as standing apart from the truth of things; what they primarily welcomed was the knowledge of the problems themselves, as contributing to the science and the discovery of the things that are. And they relied rather on the discovery of truth and on the apprehension directed towards things, and not on the keenness and sharpness of the syllogisms concerning the problems. Hence they did not pride themselves on an abundance of mathematical arguments either, but were seen to give preference to that which contributes to the discovery of things.

These, then, and others of this kind were the modes of mathematical transmission among them. And they used them scientifically and in company with theoretical philosophy, aiming at the things that are and at the beautiful, thinking that they ought always to give precedence and honour to what is limited and to what is gathered into the briefest compass, and selecting from them whatever was useful with regard to themselves and their associates and to the whole science of the things that are. For exactness in all these matters was not idly practised among them, but in order that the treatment of mathematics might hold fast to one thing, the beautiful and good, and be ordered towards one thing, the science of being and assimilation to the good. And indeed in this way it was not merely a bare knowledge of the mathematical sciences that was handed down, but a life befitting them was ordered together with it, and an ascent to the most honourable things was duly established through them. For this very reason it is worth while to practise in this way the Pythagorean occupation with the mathematical sciences, as being exceptional and preferred before all the mathematical arts.

What the definitional method of mathematics is and how it comes about, what benefit it contributes towards science, and that mathematics has an end, and what sort of thing its end is.

To this power of mathematics, then, there is another that answers as its counterpart, the definitional; for mathematics uses definitions too, and frames them with exactness. And the mode of the whole construction of definitions is this. When the divisive power of mathematics has divided according to genera and species the things in the mathematical sciences, then the definitional power gathers into one the differences that come from the division, and collects a single common account out of them all. It does the same thing also on the basis of analysis; for when analysis has led intellection up to the simpler and more common things, and has distinguished the genera and the differences as each is by nature, then synthesis, which draws together, by bringing into one the things that differ and the simple things, defines each of the things in the mathematical sciences. And thus mathematical science has the definitional account as its own, from itself, and is able to discover it theoretically. Since, then, division makes the one many and the definitional power makes the many one, in both respects it is necessary that mathematics contemplate the one, from which it sets out and to which it is led up. This, then, will be the end, which one might also call form: a one over all the many theorems; and this same thing is also beautiful and good, and it is to this that the things divided hasten to be joined.

For this reason, in the mathematical sciences too we always let go the unlimited and the particular, and hasten to ascend to what is common and determinate, all of us who practise mathematics in accordance with the doctrines of the Pythagoreans, until we have led the whole contemplation belonging to the treatment of mathematics up to the one that is the one of all the mathematical sciences together. Next after this it is worth speaking also of the customary manner of the Pythagoreans’ occupation with the mathematical sciences. They, then, detached their accounts of the mathematical sciences from sensibles, and by means of them turned discursive thought round to belief in incorporeal essence, and used them to ferry it across to the intelligibles, and considered above all what in them is fashioned in the likeness of the pure forms and the unitary reason-principles. This, then, was the manner in which they approached the theorems; and, having once removed the science of them from common and public knowledge, they made the imparting of them too, in the same way, a matter of secrecy; they shared the knowledge of them with very few, and if anything was ever divulged to the many, they expiated this as an impiety; which is why they also turned away those outside their fellowship, as being unworthy to partake of them. For Pythagoras held that one should share the philosophy contained in the mathematical sciences not with all, but only with those with whom one would share one’s whole life. And to this association he did not admit men at random, nor just anyone, but made trial of them over a long time and turned away the unworthy.

And to those outside his fellowship he did not make common the advance that had come about through him, having made the accounts of these things secret towards the others; but among those who were named Pythagoreans on account of their comradeship with him he brought about a great advance both in the philosophy concerned with the mathematical sciences and in the study of geometry, and of nearly all the things that later progressed further one would find that the beginnings came to us from him. What he prized in them was not, as some of those who came later did, the power by which men will be able to discover what has been proposed, but the theorems themselves; and among these not those that were hardest to discover, as most of the later men did, but those in which it was most possible to discern an order among them or some natural property. They were so disposed because they believed that the principles of the whole of nature are present in these things, and that here it is most easily seen what they are and how many, since these things concern a nature that is abiding and free from motion, and moreover simple; which is why they neither touched on problems, except such as were elementary, like the application of areas and squaring, nor, in the theorems, did they labour with the aim of going through everything and leaving out nothing that is possible, but sought only to see the principles themselves in each case. Their training in these sciences and their rational elaboration of them they made exact and theoretical, directed to a science proper to them; and they added to the sciences the order that befits them;

and, having received a few things at the outset, they worked these out, and brought to completion above all the most honourable and most august of the theorems; and theorems that were being practised in one way they turned round to other uses; and they established in them an order such that the simpler were handed on first and those involving composition second; and they arranged the theorems in conformity with the nature of the things that are, suitably to our capacity, appropriately to the worth of those receiving them, in agreement with the guidance towards virtue and with education as a whole, and fittingly for the purification of the soul.
Such are the marks that one might set down, on this point too, of the Pythagorean type; about which we shall say more in what will be said separately about each of the mathematical sciences.

Who the mathēmatikoi among the Pythagoreans were and in what respect they differed from the akousmatikoi, and what their work was and of what sort the form of their arguments and demonstrations.

There are two forms of the Italian philosophy, which is called Pythagorean. For there were also two kinds of those who practised it, the akousmatikoi and the mathēmatikoi. Of these, the akousmatikoi were acknowledged to be Pythagoreans by the others, but they for their part did not acknowledge the mathēmatikoi, nor that their system of study was that of Pythagoras, but rather that of Hippasus. Some say that Hippasus was a Crotoniate, others a Metapontine. But those of the Pythagoreans who are concerned with the mathematical sciences both acknowledge that these are Pythagoreans and say that they themselves are so still more, and that what they themselves say is true.

The cause of the unlikeness, they say, was as follows. Pythagoras arrived from Ionia and Samos at the time of the tyranny of Polycrates, when Italy was at its height, and the foremost men in the cities became his intimates. With the older of these, who had no leisure because they were held fast in political affairs, since it was difficult to deal with them by way of the mathematical sciences and demonstrations, he conversed in bare terms, judging that they would be benefited no less by knowing what they ought to do even without the cause, just as those under medical treatment, though they do not hear in addition why each thing must be done by them, none the less attain health. But with all the younger men he met who were able to toil and to learn, with such he dealt by way of demonstration and the mathematical sciences. They themselves, then, so they say, are descended from the latter, and those others from the former. About Hippasus they say that he was one of the Pythagoreans, but that because he was the first to divulge and to draw the sphere composed of the twelve hexagons he perished at sea as one guilty of impiety, and gained the reputation of having discovered it, whereas everything belongs to that man; for so they refer to Pythagoras and do not call him by name. The mathematical sciences advanced, once they had been divulged, two men above all carrying them forward, Theodorus of Cyrene and Hippocrates of Chios.

The Pythagoreans say that geometry was divulged in the following way. One of the Pythagoreans lost his property, and when this misfortune had befallen him he was permitted to make money from geometry. Now geometry was called by Pythagoras inquiry (historia). As regards the difference between the two systems of study, then, and as regards the mathematical sciences, this, more or less, and things of this kind, is what came about. The Pythagoreans, having devoted themselves to the mathematical sciences, and having come to love the exactness of their arguments, because these alone, of the things that men practised, possessed demonstrations, and seeing that the facts of harmony were placed beyond dispute by means of numbers, and equally the mathematical sciences concerned with sight by means of diagrams, supposed that these things and their principles were in general causes of the things that are; so that anyone who wishes to contemplate how the things that are stand must look to these, namely the numbers and the geometrical forms of the things that are, and ratios, because all things are made clear by means of them. Holding, then, that they could attach the powers of each thing to nothing more opportune or more honourable than to the causes of all things and what is primary, they went on to define the other things too in much the same manner as these. Their reductions of things to numbers and the mathematical sciences, then, were made for these reasons and seemed to them to have this pattern. Of some such kind too was their method of demonstrations, setting out from principles of this sort and possessing in this way what is trustworthy and secure in its arguments.
Chapter 26
Objections to the mathematical sciences as being of no worth, and replies to them and counter-arguments at greater length.

There have been some, both among the ancients and among the moderns, who have put forward the contrary opinion about the mathematical sciences, censuring them as utterly useless and as contributing nothing to human life. Some argue in this way: if the end of them is useless, the end for the sake of which the philosophers say one ought to learn them, then all the more must the serious pursuit of them be vain. And about the end nearly all are agreed who are reputed to have attained the greatest exactness in that pursuit. For some say that it is the science of things unjust and just and bad and good, a science similar to geometry and the others of that kind, while others say that it is the wisdom concerning nature and truth of that sort, such as Anaxagoras and Parmenides and their followers introduced. Now whoever is going to examine these matters must not fail to notice that all good things, and all things beneficial to human beings for life, consist in use and action, and not in knowing alone; for we are not healthy by being acquainted with the things productive of health, but by applying them to our bodies; nor are we wealthy by knowing wealth, but by possessing much property; nor, most important of all, do we live well by knowing certain of the things that are, but by acting well; for this is truly to be happy. So that it befits philosophy too, if indeed it is beneficial, either to be a doing of good things or to be useful for such actions.

Now that neither this nor any other of the sciences mentioned above is any kind of performance of practical affairs is plain to all; and that it is not useful for actions either, one may learn from the following. For we have a very great example in the sciences similar to it and the opinions that fall under them: of the things which the geometers contemplate through demonstration, we see them to be practitioners of none; rather, to divide a piece of land, and all the other properties of magnitudes and of places, the land-surveyors are able to deal with through experience, whereas those who are occupied with the mathematical sciences and the accounts of these things know how one ought to act, but are not able to act. The case is similar with music too and the other sciences in which the part of knowledge and the part of experience are divided and stand apart. For those who have determined the demonstrations and the syllogisms concerning concord and the other things of that kind are accustomed, like those engaged in philosophy, to inquire, but have no share in any of the works; indeed, even if they happen to be able to do something of them with their hands, as soon as they have learned the demonstrations they at once, as though on purpose, do them worse; whereas those who are ignorant of the accounts, but have been trained and opine correctly, are wholly and entirely superior for practical needs. Likewise also in what concerns astronomy, for instance about the sun and moon and the other stars, those who have studied the causes and the accounts know nothing of what is useful to human beings, whereas those who possess what these people call the nautical sciences are able to foretell to us storms and winds and many of the things that come to pass.
So that for actions such sciences will be utterly useless; and if they fall short of right actions, the love of learning falls short of the greatest goods.

In reply to these arguments, we say both that there are sciences of mathematics and that these are capable of being acquired. For both are always more knowable: what is prior than what is posterior, and what is better in nature than what is worse. For there is science of things determinate and ordered more than of their contraries, and again of causes more than of their results. Now the things in the unmoved mathematical forms are determinate and ordered. And the prior are causes more than the posterior; for when the former are done away with, the things that have their essence from them are done away with: lengths when numbers are, planes when lengths are, and solids when planes are. So that if indeed the things in the mathematical sciences are simpler than all things, they will also have more of the character of principles than all things. So that there will be sciences far more of the better and more originative things, and they are capable of being acquired; for it is far more necessary that there be wisdom of the causes and the elements than of the things posterior. For these latter are not among the highest things, nor do the first things arise by nature out of them, but it is out of those and through those that the other things too manifestly come to be and are constituted. And that to know the mathematical sciences is also the greatest of goods and the most beneficial of all the others is clear from the following. For reason and wisdom take the lead among goods; and there is no other rule and most exact standard of goods than the wise man; for whatever things he would choose, these are goods, and the contraries of these are evils.

And since all men choose most of all the things that accord with their own proper states (for the just man chooses to live justly, the man who has courage to live in accordance with courage, and the temperate man to be temperate), it is clear that in like manner the wise man too will choose the exercise of wisdom above all things; for this is the work of this faculty. So that it is evident that, according to the most authoritative judgement, wisdom is the best of goods. And it is not for the sake of use that all should pursue it; for it is in fact choiceworthy on its own account.

Concerning the benefit and the greatness of the thing I consider that enough has been demonstrated; but that the acquisition of it is far easier than that of the other goods, I am persuaded from the following. For the fact that, though no pay comes to philosophers from men for the sake of which they might labour so intensely, and though they have allowed the other arts a long start, they have nevertheless, running for a short time, passed them by in points of exactness, seems to me to be a sign of the ease that belongs to philosophy. Further, the fact that all are fond of dwelling upon it and wish to devote their leisure to it, letting go of everything else, is no small proof that close application to it comes with pleasure; for no one is willing to toil for a long time. In addition to these points, the exercise of it differs very greatly from all others: for they need neither instruments nor places for their work, but wherever in the inhabited world one sets one’s thought, from every side alike one lays hold of the truth as though it were present.
But these things have perhaps been said sufficiently for the present occasion; for it has been demonstrated both that wisdom is possible and that it is the greatest of goods and easy to acquire.

Now exact reasoning about the truth is by common consent the youngest of pursuits. For after the destruction and the flood men were compelled first to philosophise about what concerns nourishment and staying alive; then, having become better provided, they worked out the arts that aim at pleasure, such as music and those of that kind; and it was when they had more than the necessities that they then set their hand to philosophy. And those who inquire into geometry and reasonings and the other branches of education have now advanced so far, from small beginnings and in a very short time, as no other class has done in any of the arts. And yet, whereas all join in urging on the other arts, honouring them publicly and giving pay to those who possess them, those who busy themselves with these studies we not only do not encourage but often even hinder; yet all the same these studies make the greatest progress, because by nature they are the eldest; for what is later in generation takes precedence in essence and perfection.

And so the science of mathematics too prevails over the other sciences in all these respects by a wide margin, excelling all pursuits in beauty and exactness; and it is also reasonable that this should be so.

For, first, the things that are akin in nature to generation are eagerly sought after by human beings, so as to acquire them as far as they are able; but, after these, the things that release us from the corporeal nature are far more honourable than the former; for the former are presupposed as necessary, while the latter, as choiceworthy for their own sake and august, have been deemed worthy of precedence and honour. Now the mathematical sciences do contribute to us not a few uses for the whole of human life as well, as is plain to those who survey in life the works that come from the mathematical arts; nevertheless these are worthy of less serious attention, and the greatest things are the purification of the immortal soul, and the turning round of the intellect towards the intelligible, and participation in the activity of being. And mathematical science, in procuring these for us, furnishes all goods, so that I do not know whether any other method lends such help towards the end that is happiness. By these arguments, then, not only have the opposing arguments been shown to be false, but the mathematical sciences have also been demonstrated to be most useful to us.
Chapter 27
What the truly educated person ought to demand of the mathematician, and how his study is to be judged, and by what standards its correctness is to be comprehended.

Since it is the work of the educated person to be able to judge aptly what the speaker sets out well or not well, we think that the person educated in general is someone of just this kind, and that to be educated is to be able to do what has been said. It is clear, then, that in the mathematical sciences too the rightly educated person ought to demand of the mathematician correctness and his proper work, as to whether he conducts his study of them well or not well.

For just as we consider the person educated without qualification to be, though one in number, capable of judging about practically everything, so too concerning some determinate science there would be another person disposed in the same way as the one described, with respect to a part. It is clear, therefore, that for the study of the mathematical sciences too there must be certain standards of this kind, by reference to which the educated person will accept the manner of the things proved, apart from the question of how the truth stands, whether thus or otherwise. I mean, for example, whether one ought to take each single theorem of mathematics and make determinations about it by itself, for instance about these particular triangles, or whether one ought to examine the common theorems and the things that belong to all, positing them in respect of something common. For many of the same things belong to many genera that are different from one another, as for instance if one were to make the demonstration in so far as they are triangles, or in so far as they are rectilinear figures in common. For if certain things should belong, the same, to things that differ in species, the demonstration of them ought not to have any difference either. But there are perhaps other things which happen to have the same predicate, yet to differ by a difference in species; for example, the similar is one thing in the case of triangles and another in the case of numbers. And for each of the two one must make demonstrations proper to it. It must therefore be examined when one should study in common, according to genus, and when in the proper manner, according to each thing; for to have made determinations about these matters contributes a great part to mathematical education.

Further, one must demand of the mathematician his accounts in accordance with the underlying essence, and that he make the manner of his demonstrations appropriate. Just as, then, we bear with the rhetorician when he argues from what is plausible, so one must demand of the mathematician demonstrations that are necessary. But one must not seek the same necessities everywhere, nor the same exactness alike in all things; rather, just as we divide what belongs to the arts by the underlying materials, not seeking exactness alike in gold and tin and bronze, nor in cork and boxwood and lotus-wood, so in the same way in the theoretical sciences too. For the subjects will at once produce differences, whenever some are simpler and others more in composition, and some wholly unmoved and others in motion, as for instance the things in numbers and in harmony, or those in geometry and astronomy, and whenever of some the principle is intellect and of others discursive thought, while for some there are also certain slight starting-points from sense-perception, as for the heavenly things. For it is not possible to adduce the same causes, or even similar ones, concerning such things, but as far as the principles differ, so far must the demonstrations differ too; for in each of the sciences the manner is akin. Further, and at a still wider remove than these, there is the fact that some pursue their inquiry possessing principles and others not possessing them; so that here too neither similar causes nor similar accounts are to be set forth. And with a view to these matters it is necessary to know what they have that is the same and what different, and what is the same by analogy, and which kinds of science need more things and in which kinds the difficulties are more numerous; for it is roughly in these and suchlike respects that the variations in the demonstrations and accounts concerning each thing lie.

And such a study would contribute not only to judging but also to inquiring as one ought; for, possessing a determination of the cause in each case, it will produce appropriate accounts, which is not easy for one who has not been habituated to do. For nature itself by itself is able to lead the way to the principles, but is not sufficient to judge each thing unless it has acquired another understanding in addition. Further, it must be discerned whether there are several causes concerning the things about which the mathematician must speak, and which of these is by nature first and which second. For the person educated mathematically is apt to scrutinise the causes assigned as well, and to study their order.

Nor must this escape notice, that many of the more recent Pythagoreans supposed that the only things that remain the same and in the same state are the subjects of the mathematical sciences, and posited these alone as principles; and so they marked off the sciences too in the same way, as concerned with such things, and the demonstrations as well. But since we shall demonstrate, both in the discussions that now come first and in those that will be stated later, that there are many other essences too that are unmoved and remain the same, not only those of the mathematical sciences, and that those are elder and more honourable than these, and shall also demonstrate that not only are these mathematical ones principles, but there are others as well, and that those indeed are the elder and more powerful than these, and that the mathematical principles are principles not of all the things that are but of some: for these reasons mathematical demonstration now requires a determination, of what sort of things that remain the same and in the same state it is demonstrative, and from what sort of principles it syllogises, and about what sort of problems it makes its demonstrations.

For the education that passes judgement on these matters marks off both the correctness and the end of mathematics, makes its judgement of it as is fitting, and comprehends well the manner in which the inquiries ought to be conducted. So let these be our determinations on these matters too.
Chapter 28
When the problem or the manner of the demonstrations belongs to mathematics and when to another science: a scientific distinction.

Since it is often not evident whether the inquiry in hand is mathematical or belongs to another science, and since it is disputed what manner of demonstrations is mathematical, it is necessary to make clear about these matters too what sort of problems, and demonstrated in what way, display a mathematical method. In general, then, one must know beforehand that theological science and physical science lie alongside mathematical theory, so that these sciences share both their demonstrations and their problems with one another. Now the truth does indeed stand thus: the kinship of knowledge joins together a certain single affinity among the different cognitive faculties, and the things too, being in a way close to one another, possess the common continuity of the sciences with one another. Nevertheless the Pythagoreans, for their part, knit this communion together still more closely, as undivided, handing down many things about the intelligible forms by means of the mathematical sciences, and many about nature, and expounding many things about character too in a mathematical manner. But all the same one must distinguish the three genera of these accounts and determine the mathematical one separately, so that it is not confused with any of them.

Let mathematical accounts, then, be unmoved in themselves and irrefutable, fitted to the mathematical forms and genera in themselves, not comprehending these by abstraction from sensibles, but applying themselves to them in a determinate way, inasmuch as these subsist by themselves, neither having any contact with motion, nor coming together into identity with the intelligible and indivisible forms or with the intellections, but proceeding step by step in accordance with the intelligibles and the acts of discursive thought that are constituted about them, and employing this as a certain intermediate mode of knowledge. For a method of accounts and demonstrations of this kind is both mathematical and far separated from the accounts found among the other practitioners of science.
Chapter 29
On mathematical syllogisms and mathematical divisions and definitions: how mathematical science uses them, whether in its own proper manner or by taking its principles from dialectic.

It follows upon problems of this kind to examine this also along with them: how mathematical science uses division, definition and syllogisms, whether as receiving the learning of them from dialectic, or as itself exercising its activity upon them from itself. Now if it takes these over from the study concerned with reasoning, it will be in want of many things and gets the principles of its own proper knowledge from elsewhere; but if such a thing befits some other science rather than mathematical exactness, we must conceive these three, namely division, definition and syllogism, as being one thing in dialectic and another in mathematics, and as determined in each of the two according to the genus proper to each. Now those of dialectic are greater objects of study, and it is not our present purpose to go through them, whereas those proper to mathematics are the concern of mathematics itself alone.

From itself, therefore, it discovers them, perfects them and works them out; it knows well how to test what is proper to itself, and it has no need of another science for its own proper study. For it discerns not what is without qualification, as dialectic does, but the things that fall under itself; it studies them in its own proper manner, in so far as they are subject to it, and about them it makes its exact determinations; it has within itself criteria by which they must be tested; it devises several manners of demonstration, and among these it distinguishes those that are better and true and those that are ambiguous and in need of further attention. Moreover, it makes its treatment twofold, the one directed to discovery, the other to judgement. But it is capable of judgement and of discovery according to the reason peculiar to its own art, not according to the intellect that is contemplative without qualification. It is able, then, in accordance with this reason to discern how one ought to divide the species in mathematics, and what the differences are that properly divide them, and what the definitions in mathematics are, and how one ought to gather them from the mathematical divisions, and how a mathematical syllogism comes about, and by how many determinations it acquires its exactness, and when it is possible and when impossible, and in how many ways it possesses necessity. For in all these matters its own proper discovery, use and judgement need no preparation brought in from outside, as some suppose.
Chapter 30

That mathematics makes great contributions to the whole of philosophy and to all its parts, ministering to it in all things, and above all the mathematics of the Pythagoreans, which differs greatly from the rest of mathematics.

That mathematics also contributes many and great services to the whole of philosophy and to all its parts, ministering to the vision of the things that are and following along in its track, is easy to learn from what follows.

The mathematics of the Pythagoreans is not such as that which the many practise. For the latter is for the most part technical, has no single goal, and does not aim at the beautiful and good, whereas that of the Pythagoreans is pre-eminently contemplative; it refers its theorems to a single end, makes all its own accounts akin to the beautiful and good, and uses them as leading up towards being. Setting out, then, from such a starting-point, it distinguishes well within itself which of the studies belonging to it are fitted to theology, being capable of sharing in divine order and divine measures, and these it assigns to that part of philosophy; and which are appropriate to the hunt for being, with a view to affinity, commensurability and the turning round, and such theorems too it duly renders to the corresponding part. Nor does it escape its notice if some lend their aid in a scientific way to exactness of reasoning, leading the way to syllogising, demonstrating and defining well, refuting what is false and distinguishing what is true from what is false. Nor indeed is it ignorant of the harmony that is appropriate to the inquiry into nature, how it is constituted and how it is useful, how it fills up what is lacking in nature, and how it passes judgement upon these things. Further still, it descends to constitutions, the formation of characters and rightness of life, and discovers the appropriate standards of the mathematical sciences for both household and cities, and uses them as is fitting for the sake of what is best, both for correction and for the best education, for the good measure that is appropriate, and for guarding against what is shameful and acquiring what is fine, lending its aid in this way both in common, through all the mathematical sciences, and in the proper manner through each of them.

And moreover, with regard to the goods that accord with nature and to the advantages of the arts, by discovering some things, by bringing others to light as by-products and helping to establish them in the role of an addition, by furnishing works from itself and contributing parts to some, it has perfected human life, so that this is sufficient to itself and lacks nothing of what life requires. Hence we may reasonably fit the mathematics practised by the Pythagoreans together with philosophy, as being akin and well suited to it.
Chapter 31
That the Pythagoreans used the same mathematical sciences for many different things, and made several mathematical sciences indicative of the same thing, and for what reasons.

Since it is of such a kind, we find it employing along many paths the science concerning things. For it often uses the same mathematical sciences for many things, whether physical or theological, or for generation, or for the elements, or for whatever pertains to the production of generation, or for composite things, or for simple ones; for example, it uses numbers for all of these, and harmonies, and figures, and the other things of that kind; and sometimes it takes up together several at once as indicative of the same thing, for example, of the soul: numbers, harmonies, figures, and certain other mathematical objects. The cause of the former is that the natures of each of the mathematical sciences and of each mathematical essence are multiform (for this is why we use the same ones for many things, for example numbers for theological and for physical matters), while the cause of the latter is that some of the things that are have been blended from many essences and are intermediate between several extremes.

For this is why the soul and all the intermediate natures are expounded through several mathematical sciences, as being able to fit several mathematical essences and as receiving from several the confirmation of their being. These matters, then, may be taken to admit of some such account.
Chapter 32
How we sometimes treat even of sensibles mathematically, and in how many ways this comes about, and how many things in the mathematical sciences are referred to other things, and for what reasons.

It is the custom of mathematical theory sometimes to treat of sensibles too in a mathematical way, for example of the four elements geometrically or arithmetically or harmonically, and of the rest likewise. For since mathematical theory is prior by nature and sets out from things prior to those that exist by nature, for this reason it also constructs its syllogisms as demonstrative from prior causes. And it does this in several ways: either by abstraction, when, having removed the enmattered forms from matter, it examines them mathematically; or by application, when it brings the mathematical reason-principles to bear upon physical things and joins them to these; or by completion, when, by adding what is lacking, it fills out the corporeal forms, which are incomplete; or by representation, when it looks to see in what respect especially the equal and commensurable things in generation have been made like the mathematical forms; or by participation, when we examine in what respect the reason-principles that exist in other things participate in the pure reason-principles; or by reflection, whenever we observe a faint trace of the mathematical reflected in sensibles; or by division, when we apprehend the one and indivisible mathematical form as it is divided about the particulars and multiplied; or by comparison, when we examine side by side the pure forms of the mathematical sciences and those in sensibles; or by the cause that derives from prior things, when, having set up mathematical objects as causes, we examine together how the things in sensibles come to be from them.

For it is in this way, I think, that we treat mathematically of all the things in nature and in generation. And it is from this cause that many of the things in the mathematical sciences do not remain among the mathematical sciences, but are drawn to things inferior to them, either through the choice of those who use them, or also through the kinship which sensible things have with them. Sometimes, however, the starting-point taken from the mathematical sciences is also referred upwards to greater things, and to all other things, since incorporeal essence is naturally well suited to become akin to the pure essences of the things that are, and because the mathematical sciences are of a nature to be made like all things. So much, then, about these matters too.
Chapter 33

What is common in the whole of mathematical science and what is proper to it, according to the differences observed in many species, and how one must cut it according to the science of division, from one into two and then into more species.

Since the common genus of the whole of mathematical science is of the greatest importance for scientific knowledge of the present study, we must above all discern this: in what respect the whole of mathematics possesses what is common. For if we discern this one genus of it and come to know its common essence, we shall have the most perfect knowledge of it. Now we have already examined this beforehand at the beginning too, but we must also set upon the end a crown that is the same as the beginning which was laid down as foundation.
So now too let us take up again the account of the one genus of mathematical theory.

I say, then, that what is, simply so, intermediate between the intelligible and the sensible forms is the common genus of this science, containing within itself all the different species, as many and of whatever kind they are, participating primarily in the genera of being, having gathered up within itself the genera of sensibles, yet altogether surpassing these in purity, exactness, subtlety and incorporeality, and containing within itself powers of every kind, some leading up to the things that are and others inclining towards generation, and cognitions likewise. Positing this, such as it is, as one, let us conceive its differences according to the dichotomies of this intermediate nature, of which let us mark off the one as holding to being, and the other as laying hold of sensibles and standing before them; and again, taking for each of these two species different terms in turn, we shall grasp the intermediate character of the mathematical sciences in different ways, distinguishing it either according to quantity or according to some other genus of it. The distance from being, too, according as it is further off or near, will furnish the mathematical sciences with their difference. Further, the precedence among the things in the constitution of the universe, according as it is first or second, itself also produces certain differences among the mathematical sciences. And their order we ought to discover either according to succession, or according to continuity, or according to contiguity, or according to some other kind of connection.

By this constitution that proceeds from one and is multiplied, and by the ordering that is led back to one, we distinguish, and in distinguishing we likewise join together. And in this way the common essence of the mathematical sciences will be comprehended by us in common by reasoning, and divided, and led back again from the many to the one genus of mathematical essence; and this indeed is the end of the mathematical science of division and definition.
Chapter 34
Whence the science of mathematics has its name and what its character is, and to what one must attend in judging the form of the mathematical sciences.

The science of mathematics has been so named because a certain learning (mathēsis) descends into it from the intellection of the intelligibles, and this study is akin to that intellection, and learning arises about just those things with which intellection and science are concerned, and these alone among all things would be learnable (mathēta), which is why they have been called mathēmata. The Pythagoreans held that these mathematical sciences had been provided as, so to speak, proper instruments for unfolding the nature of the things that are and for removing all the mist that darkens things, so that one might behold the truth itself in its purity; and further that such learning would also help to supply the cause of the agreement in matters of character, and, becoming an ally to philosophy, would help to unveil the nature of good and evil, and that through it the commensurability of the order of the cosmos and of the circular motion of the heaven is contemplated. For this reason they thought that it was not possible to philosophise without it. Further still, it hunts down, as though through mirrors of surpassing brightness, many images of the works of nature, and this they used to name the mathematical part of philosophy, and those experienced in accounts of this sort they declared to be mathēmatikoi.

They also held that the things in the mathematical sciences are the finest paradigms of the things here, because they are regulated with reference to intellection, being stable and unmoved and always remaining the same and in the same state, so that by looking to them and imitating them one would produce in each case works that are steady and secure. The mathematical account possesses, moreover, purity, scientific character and irrefutability. And to the ancients the mathematical account seems to be prior to the physical and more originative; for on it, they supposed, the pure intellection of the other things depends. This, then, is the character of the mathematical account. And in judging its form one must attend to its exactness, its irrefutable knowledge, the correctness of its accounts and its agreement with the things that are; for it is together with these that its form shows through best. Let these too, then, be our additions to what was determined about these matters earlier.
